content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a method to eliminate the backdoor of the trojaned model. To this end, the authors propose the following procedure; Create a student model by copying and pasting the same structure as the trojaned teacher model, and random initializing the parameters. And then, using a small number of clean samples, the student model is trained with the proposed eq (1), (2) and (3) (i.e., pruning importance driven cloning). The authors have shown that the performance is higher than those of the sota models for various backdoor attacks. 

Additional experiments show that appropriately weighting the importance plays a key role in backdoor removal. A theoretical analysis of the method is also provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
- Novelty: The proposed method is intuitive and novel, although I consider Eq (1) as a form of feature knowledge distillation. Nevertheless, I believe the idea of using the importance score is novel and appropriate. 

- Ablation: Some ablation experiments show that the components of the proposed method are important. For instance, Fig. 3 shows that their form of distillation is superior in increasing the clean accuracy, while the importance score does not deteriorate it. Conversely, Fig. 4 shows that the importance score is key to lowering ASR. 

- Extensive experiments using two datasets and strong results, although the numbers for the baselines need some clarifications (please see below).

**Weaknesses** 
- One major concern is whether the baseline numbers are the results of poor finetuning of hyper-parameters or due to using augmentations during attack, which makes a stronger backdoor. For instance, in the ANP paper (Table 1), the ASR of ANP against SIG is 0.28%. While the experimental details are different (e.g. using 1% of clean data, ResNet-18), the discrepancy between the reported ASR=73.9% and 0.28% is too large. This is also the case for NAD (Table 1), which reports its ASR=3.18% against SIG, but this paper reports it to be 85.2%.
Table 2 in the appendix and Figure 5 seem to align more with the results of other papers. If this is merely due to using augmentations during attack, I believe the paper should clarify this in experimental settings. I believe using a stronger form of attack is justified especially if data augmentation is all it needs. However, I think this should be clarified at the start of the experiment section given that this drastically affects the performance.

- Is $\mu$ and $\sigma$ computed by taking the empirical mean and standard deviation across samples? How is $\sigma$ computed for the proxy variables? I am unsure of how this normalizes the gradients across layers. Can the authors please explain? 

- What other methods use additional data? I think this should be marked in the table for clarity. Do they all use the same amount of additional data (5%)? 

- As stated in the strength section, I think the proposed method is also a form of feature-level knowledge distillation (KD). Maybe the paper should distinguish itself with “logit KD” instead of “typical KD”. 

 - I would like to hear the authors’ response on these (especially the first concern) and am willing to raise the score if properly addressed.

- Possibility of misreading: Experimental setting (Sec. 5) and Table 1
How about briefly explaining the presence or absence of data augmentation in poisoning?
Table 1: It can be confusing because the values of compared methods were too different from the original paper.

- Question: I have one question on the ablation study. 
Without the set intersection, what if there is no one? i.e, if only one side is $\tau=0$.
(In other words, what if there is no activation criterion or impact criterion?)


[minor]

- Citation : batch norm under eq(2)
- (page 2, 5) What is ASR abbreviation for? It wasn't until page 8 that ASR first appeared.
- typo : figure 5. argumentation -> augmentation

content.title: Response
content.comment:
**Q1**: I believe using a stronger form of attack is justified especially if data augmentation is all it needs. However, I think this should be clarified at the start of the experiment section given that this drastically affects the performance.

> This difference is mainly due to data augmentations. We clarify the difference in Stronger Baselines section explicitly in revision.  

> The reason the reviewer still see minor difference is due to different reporting procedure, e.g.3\% in ours and 0.3% on others for SIG attack without augmentation.  We assume we don't know how backdoor looks like during training and therefore directly report the model from the last epoch for all methods. However, other papers are reporting the model with smallest backdoor attack success rate. We empirically observe large variation of attack success rate among epochs. We confirm our baseline has consistent result if using the other metric. We state the differences in Appendix experiment details.

**Q2**: Is \sigma and \mu computed by taking the empirical mean and standard deviation across samples? How is computed for the proxy variables? I am unsure of how this normalizes the gradients across layers. Can the authors please explain? 

> Yes. We compute them through the 5\% available samples.  The normalization of gradient is for consistency of different neurons. Suppose one neuron has a smaller magnitude of output range than the others. A  small gradient on this neuron will matter more than a similar gradient on an average neuron. Thus we scale this gradient by its standard deviation of this neuron. This process is formalized by the proxy variable in a theoretical way. 

**Q3**: What other methods use additional data? I think this should be marked in the table for clarity. Do they all use the same amount of additional data (5%)? 

>All methods use the same set of 5\% additional data.

**Q4**: In other words, what if there is no activation criterion or impact criterion?

>We conduct the ablation study in Appendix E.5. The result shows that combination of both criteria give the best result. If we must only choose one criterion, we find the impact criterion is more important than the activation criterion.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a defensive mechanism for removing backdoors from a model. The paper adapts knowledge distillation so that the mechanism does not only naively compare the logits between a teacher and a student but also compares the neuron activations from the intermediate layers. In this case, the teacher is the backdoored model, and the student is a network that a defender wants to train while preventing backdoors from being distilled. The paper analyzes why the naive distillation fails in the same scenario and how the new method may have the ability to "sanitize" the backdoor. In evaluation, the paper achieves superior performance on backdoor removals compared to the baselines. The paper discusses adaptive attacks and the effectiveness of the defense under configuration changes.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The paper proposes a simple yet seemingly effective defense against backdoor attacks.
2. The paper analyses why native distillation is still vulnerable to backdoor attacks.
3. The paper empirically shows that the method works more effectively than the baselines.


Weaknesses:

1. There is a huge room for improving the writing and presentations.
2. The paper claims the method is computationally efficient, but it does not provide the analysis.
3. The paper claims that the backdoor neurons can be decomposed, but not sure if it is the case based on the paper.
4. Some experiments are not clear why they are important.


Detailed comments:

I like the paper's idea of removing backdoors by "distilling only the clean model's behaviors." However, I am not sure whether this is feasible or not. The empirical evaluation shows that this is somewhat possible under the paper's threat model. 

As the evaluation is empirical, there are many questions that I think the paper should answer:


[Why do we assume that the defense is computationally efficient?]

It's empirically shown, and the paper even puts the numbers in the introduction (it takes 15 min to remove the backdoor--- I am not sure if this is wall-clock time or the time only spent for the defense). But the most important thing is to show formally that: given a backdoor (or a backdoored model), can we somewhat guarantee the removal will be done orders of magnitude faster (let's say til the point where ASR becomes below 15%)?

I believe that this should not be evaluated empirically; otherwise, in the worst case, this method can take up the same computational power as training a model from scratch on the entire data.


[How can we make sure activations from the backdoor and clean samples on the same neuron decomposed?]

The paper relies on the assumption that we can only pick the benign behaviors from the neurons (or activations), while the neuron is active for both the clean and the backdoor samples. However, I am not sure if it's feasible. If a neuron is active for both types of samples, the neuron holds a (roughly) feature that appears on both the clean and the backdoor samples. I am a bit confused about how we can separate them.

Perhaps, one can extract the neuron's activation, but nothing happens. It's because the backdoor attacks have a high specificity regarding the trigger the attacker uses. But, an adversary can easily distill the backdoor by reducing the specificity. In that case, by extracting the neuron's activation, the student can still be vulnerable to the same backdoor attacks.

The above point also makes me wonder whether the defense overfits a specific type of backdoors. I am wondering if the defense still holds with different attacks; for example, one can make a neuron active for white background, then extract any neurons activated by the white background, and the student still has the backdoor.

All those points may come from the fact that there's no guarantee a backdoor attacker will behave in a specific way. I would like to see some formal guarantee that: for any backdoor attacks, the distillation won't extract any backdoors from the teacher (or the distilled backdoor is not that strong). Not by empirically.


[Experiments That Are Not Clear]

I am not sure why we need to test the data augmentation, as there's no concrete study showing that data augmentation mitigates backdoor attacks. It's the opposite, and the data augmentation oftentimes can introduce the backdoor.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: No major concern, but I do believe that some of the claims and the list of contributions should be ironed out. For example, "we theoretically analyze the advantages of the cloning method" doesn't seem to reflect what Sec 4 is doing.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper presents a way to sanitize a backdoor from a model. It adapts knowledge distillation to achieve this goal; the adaptation also considers the neuron activations from the internal layers. The paper formally analyzes why using the logits does not lead to successful results and justifies using the internal activations. The evaluation shows the proposed defense outperforms the baselines.

I like the idea of this paper, but the claims are just built on empirical observation, or they claim more than it has to be. Here are my major concerns:

1. The paper claims the method is computationally efficient, but it does not provide the analysis.
2. The paper claims that the backdoor neurons can be decomposed, but not sure if it is the case based on the paper.
3. Some experiments are not clear why they are important.

and I am happy to update my score if those concerns are addressed.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you again for your great inputs. Based on you proposal, we include two more proofs to strengthen our analysis in Appendix B and C.

**Q1**: In theory, how to show defense is computationally efficient?

>Thanks for the deep question. In the revision, we theoretically prove our method is computationally faster than training from scratch and distilling from logits, given certain assumptions. 
The intuitive explanation is as follows. From theorem 2, our method has a much smaller sample complexity than training from scratch and distilling from logits. A smaller sample complexity implies fewer samples needed for training given the same accuracy and hence less computation. The proof can be found in Appendix B.

**Q2**: If a neuron is active for both types of samples, the neuron holds a (roughly) feature that appears on both the clean and the backdoor samples. I am a bit confused about how can we make sure activations from the backdoor and clean samples on the same neuron decomposed?

> The short answer is that we can’t make sure those neurons are decomposed. However, our method will still work in this situation when the neurons are not separable.
The reasons are as follows.
First, even the clean samples and backdoor samples activate the same set of neurons, the activation value patterns can be different. We only copy the benign activation patterns using a small set of clean samples.

>Secondly, if the activation patterns are similar, those patterns may contribute differently between backdoor samples’ result and clean samples’ result. Therefore, we only copy the activations that result in benign classifications, through impact criterion.

>Lastly, we have adaptive attacks that proactively aim to bypass our defense by aligning benign and poisoned activation values. Specifically, adaptive attack 2 in Table 1 optimizes a trigger that maximizes the cloning loss. In another word, it enlarges those important activations. The results show that our method is still effective even under such strong attacks. 

**Q3**: I would like to see some formal guarantee that: for any backdoor attacks, the distillation won't extract any backdoors from the teacher.

> Suggested by the reviewer, we show that for a family of backdoor attacks, our method guarantees the removal of the backdoor. However, fine-tuning based method may not guarantee this. Moreover, the importance of cloning will accurately identify the compromised neuron. Our proof can be found in Appendix C.

> However, we believe to prove this point for any potential backdoors may be fundamentally challenging. Specifically, we find difficulties in modeling different backdoor attacks using a uniform constraint. And we find describing the effect of backdoor on internal neurons difficult. 

**Q4**: All those points may come from the fact that there's no guarantee a backdoor attacker will behave in a specific way … (or the distilled backdoor is not that strong).

> We agree with the reviewer that we cannot guarantee the removal of backdoors for all possible backdoors. However, we believe we have made good progress towards the goal compared with recent works like ANP and NAD. We propose a promising and novel approach. Different from all previous works, we show training from scratch is an effective way to remove backdoors. We achieve better results and have extensive theoretical analysis on certain aspect of our method.  

**Q5**: I am not sure why we need to test the data augmentation, as there's no concrete study showing that data augmentation mitigates backdoor attacks. It's the opposite, and the data augmentation oftentimes can introduce the backdoor.

> We include data augmentation for stronger backdoor baselines. We found the effectiveness of many baselines are greatly affected when presenting the backdoor model with stronger data augmentation.  We thus include the stronger baselines for better evaluation. We will change the description for clarity.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposed a defense model for backdoor attacks. The main goal of this paper is to advocate model cloning versus
knowledge distillation in defense techniques for backdoor threats and all the discussions and experiments are devoted to support this hypothesis
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Overall the paper presentation is very systematic and covers the state-of-the-art research works on backdoor attacks. The authors attempted to support their discussions both theoretically and through experiments. The empirical results show that the proposed defense mechanism significantly outperforms the competitors.

However, I have some concerns regarding the presentation and discussions that are detailed below:
1- In Theorem 2, a refined bound for empirical Rademacher complexity of cloned model is obtained. I checked the proofs and it remained unclear to me why the same proof cannot be used for the distilled model. My understanding is that the proof is not very tailored to the structure of the proposed algorithm and the inequalities might hold for the distilled model too.

2- In Figure 6, \lambda = 0.1 corresponds to enforcing the clone loss weakly. However, the figure shows that while the clean accuracy
for this case significantly drops, the ASR is zero for all the temperature values \tau. As the goal is to advocate the cloned model, it is not
clear for me why the model turns out to be significantly resistant to the backdoor attack while the clone loss is enforced weakly.

3- I was wondering how much setting the weights in the clone loss in the way proposed in the paper are crucial for gaining performance and if there is any degradation when the weights w_i are simply set to one in the proposed clone loss.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is not very clear and there are some missing parts. Since there are many acronyms and notations in the paper, I would encourage the authors to create a table of all the notations so that it makes it easier for the reader to follow the paper.
Above that, there are some missing information:
- The acronym ASR is used first time without definition.
- This sentence requires a citation "if a trojaned model is substantially overfit on a trigger, fine-tuning may not be able to remove the
backdoor without lengthy retraining."
- The authors claimed if a neuron is important for both benign and poisoned samples, the proposed method copy its
behaviors for benign inputs. But they did not provide any evidence for that.
- What is n in Lemma 3?
- Which backdoor attack is used in Figure 5?
- L_{clone} needs to be defined in the body of paper.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I believe the three points that I discussed in the last part are needed to be clarified and without clarification/justification of these points it is
difficult to evaluate the significance of the work. I would be happy to enhance my score upon addressing the points that I listed before.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks again for your great efforts.

**Q1**: I checked the proofs and it remained unclear to me why the same proof cannot be used for the distilled model. 

> The reviewer has a precise understanding of our theorem. The bound itself holds for both the distilled model and the cloned model. However, part of the bound  for cloned model is not constrained during distilled model optimization. This factor makes the bound for cloned model somewhat redundant when applying for distilled model.

**Q2**:  As the goal is to advocate the cloned model, it is not clear for me why the model turns out to be significantly resistant to the backdoor attack while the clone loss is enforced weakly.

> This phenomenon actually supports the strength of our method. The great effectiveness reviewer observed is because we train the model from scratch on clean data, different from fine-tuning based method. We are the first to try this training-from-scratch approach to remove backdoors. This almost guarantees the removal of backdoor attacks. However it has one shortcoming that the clean accuracy will be greatly reduced. Thus we further include cloning to improve accuracy without recovering backdoor behaviors.

**Q3**:  I was wondering how much setting the weights in the clone loss in the way proposed in the paper are crucial for gaining performance and if there is any degradation when the weights w_i are simply set to one in the proposed clone loss.

> The result of setting w_i to 1 corresponds to the case with  temperature 0 in Figure 4. We can observe that a large portion of backdoor behavior will remain using 1 as w_i. And using our proposed weight will however greatly reduce the attack success rate.

**Q4**: Some clarifications: 

> n in lemma 3 is the size of samples. We use CleanLabel attack on CIFAR-10 in Figure 4.  We change the sentence ""if a trojaned model is substantially overfit on a trigger, fine-tuning may not be able to remove the backdoor without lengthy retraining." It is now supported by our experiments.
